```{R}
library(koma)
set.seed(1)
```

# Overview

`koma` models quarter-on-quarter (qoq) growth rates. Some relationships are better
described with year-over-year growth, e.g. wages, which are often indexed to
the inflation of the past year. This vignette adds year-over-year inflation to
a wage equation with an identity of qoq growth rates.

Let \(P_t\) be the consumer price level in quarter \(t\). With
`method = "diff_log"`, the year-over-year growth rate is the sum of the last
four qoq growth rates \(\pi_t = 100\,\Delta \ln P_t\):
\[
\pi^{yoy}_t = 100\,(\ln P_t - \ln P_{t-4})
= \pi_t + \pi_{t-1} + \pi_{t-2} + \pi_{t-3} .
\]
With `method = "percentage"` the sum is only an approximation.

# Model

```{R}
equations <- "inflation ~ inflation.L(1),
n_wages ~ inflation_yoy + n_wages.L(1),
inflation_yoy == inflation + inflation.L(1:3)"

sys_eq <- system_of_equations(equations)
print(sys_eq)
```

Variables enter the equations as qoq growth rates: `inflation` is qoq inflation
\(\pi_t\) and `n_wages` is nominal wage growth.

# Data

We use the U.S. data in `klein`. `inflation` holds the PCE deflator, computed
from nominal and real consumption, as a level; `rate()` turns it into qoq
inflation.
`inflation_yoy` is endogenous and needs data too; it is already a growth rate,
so `series_type = "rate"`, and `method = "none"` because its level is the
price level, which `inflation` already holds.

```{R}
deflator <- klein$n_consumption / klein$consumption * 100

ts_data <- list(
    inflation = as_ets(deflator, series_type = "level", method = "diff_log"),
    n_wages = as_ets(klein$n_wages, series_type = "level", method = "diff_log"),
    inflation_yoy = as_ets(100 * diff(log(deflator), lag = 4),
        series_type = "rate", method = "none"
    )
)
```

# Estimation

The sample starts in 1972 to include the inflation swings of the 1970s and
1980s.

```{R}
dates <- list(
    estimation = list(start = c(1972, 1), end = c(2019, 4)),
    forecast = list(start = c(2024, 1), end = c(2025, 4))
)

estimates <- estimate(ts_data, sys_eq, dates)
summary(estimates, variables = "n_wages")
```

# Forecast

We end the data in 2023 Q4, the quarter before the forecast.

```{R}
estimates$ts_data[sys_eq$endogenous_variables] <-
    lapply(sys_eq$endogenous_variables, function(x) {
        stats::window(estimates$ts_data[[x]], end = c(2023, 4))
    })

forecasts <- forecast(estimates, dates)
print(forecasts)
```

A change in qoq inflation enters `inflation_yoy` for four quarters. The
forecast of `inflation_yoy` is the sum of the last four qoq rates, including
the observed ones at the start:

```{R}
inflation <- stats::ts(
    c(
        stats::window(rate(ts_data$inflation), end = c(2023, 4)),
        rate(forecasts$mean$inflation)
    ),
    end = c(2025, 4), frequency = 4
)
cbind(
    inflation_yoy = forecasts$mean$inflation_yoy,
    sum_of_quarters = stats::window(
        stats::filter(inflation, rep(1, 4), sides = 1),
        start = c(2024, 1)
    )
)
```

# Notes

If the model already has the log price level, e.g. for an error-correction
term as in `vignette("koma-error-correction")`, the same rate can be defined as
`inflation_yoy == p_level - p_level.L(4)`.

Keep year-over-year rates on the right-hand side. As the dependent variable of
a stochastic equation, consecutive values share three quarters, so the
residuals are correlated over time, and koma cannot rebuild levels from them.
